title: Harm reduction approaches for the use of benzodiazepines: A scoping review

claims.statement: In people who use benzodiazepines (prescribed, diverted, counterfeit or novel 'designer' benzodiazepines, most often together with opioids, stimulants or alcohol), evidence is insufficient to say whether any harm reduction service or policy lowers harm. As described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources found up to July 2025, which mapped them without appraising them (Morrison et al., 2025), the approaches studied were drug checking (11 sources), prescribed benzodiazepines as treatment or safer supply (5), policies on scheduling, prescribing and surveillance (9) and approaches for particular groups (10); by the designs listed in the review's table, 17 were quantitative pilot, retrospective, cross-sectional or similar studies, 9 qualitative, 4 mixed-methods, 4 reviews and 1 a policy analysis, and none was a randomized trial. Most drug-checking sources tested how well laboratory methods detect benzodiazepines: in 59 samples, a portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometer identified 36% of those containing etizolam (78% when etizolam was more than 3% of the sample by weight), against 9% with infrared spectroscopy. At one Canadian service, infrared analysis found alprazolam in 33 of 139 samples (23.7%) that people expected to be alprazolam (Xanax), and of 20 sent for confirmatory testing, 14 contained other active ingredients only. In a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, among 68 of 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore followed up a month after receiving fentanyl test strips, reported using alone fell from 96% to 68% and benzodiazepine use from 22% to 7%. Prescribed benzodiazepines were described for 6 of 77 residents of COVID-19 isolation hotels, whose programme as a whole reported no overdoses, and for more than 70 people experiencing homelessness in Dublin, from whom no feedback was collected; in one inner-London general practice, opioid substitution patients maintained on benzodiazepines (127 of 278) stayed in treatment longer (72 months against 34 and 51) and had a lower death rate in treatment (1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years) than the others, but a larger rise in deaths after leaving treatment, by figures the review reports inconsistently. After Australia moved alprazolam to a stricter schedule in 2014, four of five evaluations summarized in a 2021 review reported large falls in alprazolam use and harms, including overdose deaths, while figures the authors cite from a letter, without definitions, show benzodiazepine overdose deaths overall rising from 160 in 2009 to 238 in 2015. After the United Kingdom rescheduled temazepam gel capsules, 100 people interviewed described less injecting of capsules but continued injecting of tablets, higher prices and substitution with flunitrazepam. The authors find harm reduction largely missing for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimates. Detection: portable gas chromatography–mass spectrometry 36% of etizolam-containing samples (78% above 3% by weight) against 9% with infrared (59 samples); a miniature mass spectrometer quantified etizolam in 11 of 15 samples that strips and/or infrared had failed to detect or quantify. Expected alprazolam: 33 of 139 (23.7%) by infrared; of 20 confirmed, 2 alprazolam alone, 4 alprazolam with other ingredients, 14 other ingredients only. Toronto: benzodiazepine-type drugs in 116 of 555 samples, 15 of them expected to be benzodiazepines; benzodiazepine-type drugs present in 24 (41%) of samples linked to a negative effect (presence, not cause). After test strips (pilot, 68 of 103 followed up): using alone 96% to 68%, benzodiazepine use 22% to 7%; 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour. Prescribed benzodiazepines: 6 of 77 hotel residents; more than 70 people in Dublin. Opioid substitution case notes: retention 72 against 34 and 51 months; in-treatment mortality 1.31 against 1.79 per 100 patient-years; post-treatment rate in the maintained group 5.90 per 100 years, reported as a 450% rise (4.5 times the in-treatment rate, an increase of about 350%, editors' calculation). Alprazolam rescheduling: 4 of 5 evaluations reported large declines; alprazolam-related deaths 57 (2012) to 23 (2015); benzodiazepine overdose deaths 160 (2009) to 238 (2015). Kentucky 'no benzodiazepine' formulary: prescriptions down 89% over two years. Victoria emergency departments, 2020 to 2022: novel benzodiazepine-type drugs in 183 of 1112 drug-toxicity presentations (16.5%). Poison-centre line: safety information to 6635 of 17,616 callers (37.7%), no outcome evaluation.

claims.statement: In people who use benzodiazepines, evidence is insufficient to say whether anything they do themselves before or during use lowers harm: as described second-hand in a 2025 scoping review of 35 sources that did not appraise them (Morrison et al., 2025), no source compared people who used such a practice with people who did not. Practices appear only as people's accounts or researchers' recommendations: in a study of a Swedish online drug forum about flubromazolam (122 in the review's table), posters described limiting their own access to the drug while intoxicated, staying at home, limiting how often they used, avoiding alcohol at the same time and comparing vendors and batches; in British Columbia during COVID-19, women and gender-diverse people who use drugs (45, interviewed) formed informal peer networks to check on one another because of benzodiazepine contamination and the risk of sexual assault; in an ethnography in Melbourne, one participant described using temazepam at home to avoid losing money or drugs, or being arrested, while sedated; and the authors of a survey of 252 people who inject drugs in Bangkok called for education against injecting alone. The only numbers come from a before-and-after pilot without a comparison group, in which 103 women who do sex work and use drugs in Baltimore received fentanyl test strips: of the 68 followed up a month later, 69% reported doing something to lower harm after a result, such as asking someone to check on them, and reported using alone fell from 96% to 68%. The review searched on terms such as harm reduction and did not cover peer-led resources, so practices described elsewhere may be missing; its authors find harm reduction largely absent for people who are not seeking abstinence or treatment. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: No comparison and no effect estimate. The only numbers: in a before-and-after pilot of fentanyl test strips (68 of 103 followed up at one month, no control group), reported using alone was 96% before and 68% after, and 69% reported a harm reduction behaviour after a result.
